vectors.description: Host conformance positive control (§16.3): a well-behaved verifier returns a bare `allow` at exit 0 and the host-under-test MUST relay `allow`. Proves the host-conformance suite is not vacuously always-deny.

Host conformance positive control (§16.3): a well-behaved verifier returns a schema-valid `deny code=expired` at exit 0. The host MUST relay the deny with the verifier's code and MUST NOT attach a host failure_class — this is the verifier's decision, not a fail-closed override.
Offered case (1) malformed stdout (§5.2/§7.2): the verifier writes non-JSON to stdout at exit 0. The host MUST fail closed.

Offered case (1) malformed stdout, single-object framing (§5.2/§7.2): the verifier writes TWO concatenated JSON verdicts. A lenient parser that reads only the first object is forbidden; the host MUST fail closed.
Offered case (1) malformed stdout, verdict schema (§3.4/§7.2): the verifier writes valid JSON whose `verdict` is neither allow nor deny. The host MUST fail closed.

Registry closure (§3.4/§9/§7.2): the verifier returns an otherwise well-formed `deny` whose `code` is not in the §9 registry. The §3.4 deny schema closes `code` over the registry enum, so the verdict fails the schema and the host MUST fail closed with `schema_invalid`. The host MUST NOT relay the unknown code as a verifier decision — a broken or hostile verifier must not be able to mint denial semantics the contract never defined.
Offered case (1) malformed stdout, verdict schema (§3.3/§3.4/§7.2): a `deny` verdict missing the REQUIRED `code`/`message`. The host MUST fail closed.

Offered case (1) malformed stdout, single-object parse (§5.2/§7.2): a valid `allow` verdict followed by trailing non-JSON bytes. Trailing bytes after the one object are a fail-closed condition; the host MUST NOT act on the leading allow.
Offered case (2) timeout / no output (§6/§7.2): the verifier reads stdin, writes nothing, and never exits. The host owns the timeout; it MUST kill the process and deny.
Offered case (2) timeout / no output (§6/§7.2): the verifier writes a partial JSON verdict then hangs forever. No complete object arrives and the process never exits; the host timeout MUST fire.

Offered case (3) nonzero exit (§7.1/§7.2/§16.4): the verifier prints a syntactically valid `allow` and then exits NON-ZERO. Exit status is part of the contract; the host MUST treat this as deny and MUST NOT act on the stdout allow.

Offered case (3) killed-by-signal (§7.2): the verifier terminates via an unsolicited fatal signal before producing a verdict. The host MUST treat this as deny. The process both dies by signal AND leaves stdout empty — both are §7.2 fail-closed conditions — so a conforming host may report either `signal_death` (checks termination first, like the reference host) or `unparseable_stdout` (checks the empty stdout first).
Offered case (4) oversize output (§6/§7.2): the verifier floods stdout past the host's output bound. The host MUST bound the read, kill the process, and deny — it MUST NOT buffer unboundedly.

Offered case (5) reserve-before-act (§7.3/§16.5): in host nonce mode the verifier returns `allow` with `consume_nonces`. With an empty durable store the host MUST reserve every nonce THEN allow. Observable: decision=allow AND the nonce is durably present in the store afterwards.

Offered case (5) reserve-before-act, replay (§7.3/§16.5): the same allow+consume_nonces verdict, but the nonce is ALREADY in the durable store. The host MUST reject as replay even though the verifier returned allow — proving reservation happens before the host acts on the verdict.

Offered case (5) reserve EVERY entry (§7.3/§16.5): an allow carrying TWO nonces where only the second is already reserved. Because ANY conflict is a replay, the host MUST deny — proving it reserves the whole list, not just the first entry.

Offered case (1) malformed stdout, closed verdict schema (§3.4/§7.2): an `allow` carrying a disallowed additional property. The §3.4 schema is closed (additionalProperties:false); the host MUST fail closed rather than ignore the unknown field.

Offered case (1) malformed stdout, verdict `kind` enum (§3.5/§7.2): an `allow` with a `kind` outside classical|zk|external. §7.2 requires the host to treat an unrecognized `kind` as a malformed verdict and fail closed.

Offered cases (1)+(5), verdict schema (§3.2/§3.4/§7.2): an `allow` with an EMPTY `consume_nonces` array. The schema requires minItems:1 (the key is omitted when there is nothing to burn); the host MUST fail closed.

Offered cases (1)+(5), verdict schema (§3.2/§3.4/§7.2): an `allow` whose `consume_nonces` entry omits the REQUIRED `issuer_key` and `retain_until`. The host MUST validate the full closed schema and fail closed — it MUST NOT reserve a partial nonce entry.

Offered case (1) malformed stdout, closed deny schema (§3.4/§7.2): a `deny` verdict carrying a disallowed additional property. The deny shape is closed; the host MUST fail closed rather than relay an unrecognized field.

Offered cases (1)+(5), closed consume_nonces entry schema (§3.2/§3.4/§7.2): an `allow` whose nonce entry carries a disallowed additional property. The host MUST validate each entry as a closed object and fail closed — it MUST NOT reserve an entry with unrecognized fields.

Offered cases (1)+(5), consume_nonces entry field types (§3.2/§3.4/§7.2): an `allow` whose nonce entry has a string `retain_until` instead of an integer. The host MUST validate entry field types and fail closed.

Offered case (1) malformed stdout, the literal `garbage bytes` variant (§5.2/§7.2): the verifier writes raw, non-UTF-8 bytes (not valid-UTF-8 text) to stdout at exit 0. A conforming host MUST decode/parse defensively and fail closed rather than crash or mis-handle the invalid bytes. Distinct from non-json-stdout.js, which writes valid UTF-8 text.

Offered cases (1)/(2) malformed stdout, single-object parse (§5.2/§7.2): a non-JSON PREFIX before an otherwise-valid `allow`. §5.2 forbids a leading/trailing prefix around the object; allow-trailing-garbage.js covers the suffix, this covers the LEADING prefix. The host MUST NOT extract the embedded allow — it MUST fail closed.

Offered cases (2)/(5) wall-clock timeout, hard-deadline variant (§6/§7.2/§16.3): the verifier WOULD emit a valid `allow` at exit 0, but only after sleeping far past the host deadline. The host timeout is a hard wall-clock deadline, not just a hang detector: the host MUST kill at the deadline and deny `timeout`, never observing the late allow. Sharper than no-output-hang.js (which never produces output).

Offered case (6) verify `kind` (§3.5), acceptance side: a well-behaved `allow` self-describing as `kind=classical`. `kind` is OPTIONAL and, when present, MUST be one of classical|zk|external. The host MUST accept every valid kind and relay `allow`, not just the default `zk`. Acceptance counterpart to host-deny-bad-kind; proves the host validates the closed enum without hard-coding one value.

Offered case (6) verify `kind` (§3.5), acceptance side: a well-behaved `allow` self-describing as `kind=external` — the class a third-party (non-Bolyra) verifier declares. The host MUST accept it and relay `allow`, catching a host that hard-codes acceptance of only zk/classical and would wrongly reject a valid external verdict.

Host conformance (§7.2, §16.3): the verifier writes a complete, schema-valid, newline-terminated `allow`, flushes it to fd 1, and is then terminated by an unsolicited fatal signal (SIGABRT raised from its own teardown, the native-library crash path §5.1 anticipates) before ever calling exit. §7.2 requires the host to treat death by signal as deny 'regardless of what (if anything) reached stdout', and to classify it as `signal_death`, distinct from `nonzero_exit`. Catches the stdout-first fail-open host: it parses the perfect verdict, then guards the exit status with `code > 0` (or equivalent), which a signal death bypasses because Node's close event reports `code === null` and Python's returncode is negative. Signal sibling of `host-deny-nonzero-exit-after-allow`; unlike `host-deny-killed-by-signal`, the verdict here is fully delivered before death.

Host conformance positive control (§3.3, §3.5): a well-behaved verifier returns a schema-valid `allow` carrying an explicit `"kind":"zk"` at exit 0. §3.5 states that a `zk`-class verifier MAY omit the field and that "emitting `"kind":"zk"` explicitly is equivalent for a revision-aware host"; §3.3 permits `kind` on either verdict. The host MUST relay `allow` and MUST NOT treat the explicit default class as an unrecognized `kind` (the §7.2 fail-closed path applies only to values outside the {classical, zk, external} enum). Catches a host that whitelists only the two non-default classes, or that accepts `zk` solely by absence of the field.
Verifier envelope (§2.1): stdin is not JSON at all. Every conforming verifier, regardless of proof domain, MUST yield deny code=malformed_input in a single closed §3.4 verdict at exit 0 (§5.1, §7.1).
Verifier envelope (§2.1): empty stdin (immediate EOF) is not a JSON object. MUST yield deny malformed_input; the verdict itself must still be a well-formed single object at exit 0.
Verifier envelope (§2.1): stdin is valid JSON but not an object (an array). 'A request that is not a JSON object ... MUST yield deny code=malformed_input.'

Verifier envelope (§2, §2.1): two concatenated request objects on stdin. The host MUST write exactly one object (§2); the concatenation is not a single JSON object, so the verifier MUST classify it malformed_input rather than parsing leniently.
Verifier envelope (§2.1): a valid request object followed by trailing non-whitespace bytes is not a single JSON object. MUST yield deny malformed_input.
Verifier envelope (§2.1): request missing the REQUIRED bundle field. 'A request that is ... missing a REQUIRED field ... MUST yield deny code=malformed_input.'

Verifier envelope (§2.1, §2.2): bundle present but empty. The normative request schema requires minLength 1 ('bundle (string, REQUIRED, non-empty)'), so the request MUST be denied — but §2.1's malformed_input trigger list ('not a JSON object, missing a REQUIRED field, or a field of the wrong type') does not literally cover present-but-empty, and the contract does not bind this violation to a specific code. The vector therefore asserts only the fixed part: a deny, in the closed §3.4 envelope (which itself restricts code to the §9 registry), at exit 0.
Verifier envelope (§2.1): granted_capabilities is a string, not an array of strings. 'A request that ... has a field of the wrong type MUST yield deny code=malformed_input.'

Verifier envelope (§2.1, §2.2): now_unix is 0, violating the normative schema's exclusiveMinimum 0 ('now_unix (integer, REQUIRED, positive)'). The field is present and integer-typed, so §2.1's malformed_input trigger list does not literally apply and the contract fixes the deny but not the code. The vector asserts a deny in the closed §3.4 envelope at exit 0.

Verifier envelope (§2.1, §11): a request satisfying every §2.1 structural requirement except that version is 2. 'A well-formed request whose version is not 1 MUST yield deny code=unsupported_version.' Exact-code assertion: a verifier that classifies every bad input malformed_input does not implement version negotiation and fails here.
